I've signed up for a couple of those class-action suits. Basically the impression I got is some gigantic corporation commits some great misdeed against a bunch of its customers and a gigantic law firm sues them. If/when the case is settled any actual money goes to the lawyers and the class-action "plaintiffs" get like a fiver$. Had another great session skating this week. This might not be as impressive as the wall ride I did last week, but I've been trying for months to be able to drop back into a transition after a grind so this was a huge accomplishment for me. I think this week's project will be to try to extend the length of the grind.

What is the appeal of this? Genuine curiosity. It's just not immediately apparent to me why people enjoy the whole skating thing. I would love to hear you explain why it makes you passionate. Is it the danger of the concrete?

I can only speak for myself, but I do it because I love how dynamic the sport is in how you navigate the obstacles and the flow of gliding around the park. Then there's the feeling you get from landing a new trick that you've been working on for months. When it finally clicks and you lace a new grind or spin, you feel unstoppable.

There is a bit of an adrenaline rush that comes from the danger aspect of the concrete. But I really only feel that part when I'm dropping in on a vert transition or trying air over a gap that's bigger than I've done before. But that's more of an overcoming fear thing. I wear pads and a helmet, and I know how to fall correctly to keep from injuring myself more than some bruising, so it's more of a mental thing than physical danger.

At the end of the day, it's about pushing myself to improve and get a little bit better than when I started the session.

I definitely get the last part. I figure there is a pursuit of accomplishment and skills. So is skating, then, a choice of convenience as opposed to skiing, for example, which has a similar aspect of "flow" and obstacles, but may be harder to access in terms of facilities and equipment? Or is there something about skating in particular that is special or that draws you? I love cello because the specific sound of it and the way you handle the instrument resonates with me in a way that clarinet doesn't even though both offer the same pursuit and challenges of being instruments. I love golf because it appeals to the individualist perfectionist in me likes the challenge of millimetre technique and complete concentration in a game against yourself. See, I don't get excited for horse racing, but I immediately see the attraction of being one with your animal and training and extracting the absolute limit of timing and performance in that sprint. When I look at skating, I see something that's certainly harder than it looks, but I don't see what makes people fall in love with it.

I don't see it as a convenience thing, but I have heard of skiers who use skating as a way to practice in the off season. But I think that one of the draws is more of the community aspect too. In reality, skating is a solo activity, but when you go to a skatepark and start working on a line or trying to nail a particular trick, you have the other skaters around you cheering you on or helping you figure out what you're doing wrong to help you lace the trick you just bailed out on.

I guess I like it because of the sense of speed, grace, and freedom I get when skating plus the community of skaters are a bunch of nice and supportive folks. Especially since none of those dickhead skateboarders from the 90s who chased out the inline crowd and pushed us underground are around any more.

As a more fph friendly reason, it's also a fairly shitlordy sport since you have to be fairly fit in order to perform anything more advanced than skating backwards.

@Rokuah summed it up pretty well. Skating doesn't have a whole ton of practical value, kind of like dancing. For me it's something that's fun, challenging, and never gets old. That feel/sound of your wheels vibrate on concrete on a good-weather day around the lake is just euphoric. The danger aspect does give you a bit of a kick. I was a downhill longboarder (think more surfing than Tony Hawk - I might be able to do a really crappy ollie if I tried, LOL) and you really have to be fearless. I don't do the crazy high-speed shit anymore, switched from my suicidal Fluid pintail to a drop-through when I broke my arm.

It does build an absolutely indomitable sense of inner-ear/balance. I dare any fucking person to try to tip me over!!

I wear pads and a helmet too, LOL. I advise kids to do the same every time I see them bounce off the pavement like I used to do in my teens and 20s. The power and beauty of youth... hahah. I'll never stop skating. Just better at gauging the risks now.
